This is game 20 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (17,168 bytes)
- games.md (31,786 bytes)
- libs.py (813 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Usage: python3 libs.py <<< "board rows 9..1 as 9 lines of X/O/." ; prints groups and liberties
import sys
cols="ABCDEFGHJ"
rows=[l.split() for l in sys.stdin.read().strip().splitlines()]
rows=[r[1:10] if len(r)>9 else r for r in rows]
B={}
for i,r in enumerate(rows):
    for j,c in enumerate(r): B[(j,9-i)]=c
def nb(p):
    x,y=p
    for q in((x+1,y),(x-1,y),(x,y+1),(x,y-1)):
        if q in B: yield q
seen=set()
for p in B:

                elif B[q]==B[p] and q not in seen: seen.add(q);g.append(q)
            k+=1
        n=lambda s:",".join(sorted(cols[a]+str(b) for a,b in s))
        print(B[p],n(g),"libs:",len(libs),n(libs))

## Game 16 — White vs 16k — WIN W+4 (White 39 area + 7 = 46 vs 42). FIRST WHITE WIN.
Moves: B G6, W C4, B D7, W E5! (center point between B's two stones), B F5 (attach), W F4
(hane under), B G4, W F3 (F4 had 2 libs; solid, makes E4 cut fail), B D5, W E4 (E5 had 2
libs), B D4 (wedge), W D3! (keeps C4 linked to bottom; B D4-D5 down to 2 libs), B E6, W C5
(atari, B D6 forced), B D6, W G3 (protect bottom-right + my group's libs), B H4, W C6, B C7,
W B7 (hane), B B8, W B6 (B7 had 2 libs), B C9, W H3, B J3, W J2 (atari), B J4, W H2 (stops
B H2 atari trick on J2), B A7, W A6 (atari, sente), B A8, W C3 (fills cut, free), B pass,
W H7 invasion (free; died: B G8, W H8, B H6, W J6, B J5, W J7, B G7 -> 2 libs), pass pass.
Takeaways:
- vs B 3-4 G6 + D7 framework: W C4 then E5 (tengen) split black's stones; black's attach F5
  -> W hane F4 under it, then fix every 2-lib stone SOLIDLY (F3, E4) before anything else.
  Result = clean rows 1-3 + left cols A-C up to row 6 = 39. The wall E4/E5/F4 faced black but
  was attached to my bottom area, so it was never a sandwiched wall.
- Wedge D4 between C4/E4: answer D3 (underneath) — C3/E3 cuts both fail, and it attacks
  the wedge (2 libs) so C5 atari next is sente.
- Order of big boundary moves: G3 (bottom right, also my libs) > C6 (left side up) > B7 hane
  > H3 > J2 atari. Each 2-lib hane stone got its connection right away (B6, H2).
- Late free invasion (H7) behind black's top wall died as usual (eye space only J8/J9/H9).

## Game 17 — Black vs 12k — LOSS (resigned move 61, ~33 area vs 48)
Moves: B C4, W G3, B G6, W D3 (approach under), B D4, W C3, B F4, W F3, B G4, W C6 (invasion
of my top), B C5, W F7 (!! top framework C6+F7), B D7 (split), W D6, B E7, W E6, B F6, W F8,
B C7, W B7, B B6? (2-lib cutting stone), W B5 (atari), B E5, W A6 (captures B6), B B8, W B4,
B D5, W B6 (connects; group alive via edge + B3 link), B E8, W A8, B G7, W E9, B G8, W C8,
B F9 (captured F7/F8), W B9 (captured B8), B D9, W D8, B E3, W E2, B E4, W H3, B H4, W J4,
B J5, W J3, B E9, W H5 (J5 atari), B H6, W J6 (captured J5), B J7, W J5, B G5, W H1,
B G2 (probe), W H2, B C9, W B8 (eyes A7+A9), B F2, W D2, resign.
Takeaways:
- Rows 1-3 strip for W (27) + komi = 34, so as Black I had a WON position at move 10 if I
  held all of rows 4-9. But a 6-row-high open top is TOO BIG to hold: W C6 then F7 built a
  top framework. My one stone G6 could not cover rows 6-9. After W's low approach (D3/C3 under
  my row-4 wall), the next big point is a TOP stone (D7/E7 or C7), not more row-4 stones
  (F4/G4 were slow: W wasn't threatening the 4th line yet). Lesson G7 again: pre-empt with a
  3rd-line-from-top stone (D7/F7) once my bottom wall is solid.
- My answer to the invasion C6 (C5, solid) was OK; then W F7 and the fight D7/E7/F6 made a
  mess where my 3 top stones and W's center group were both weak. W's center connected to the
  LEFT EDGE (B7, B5, A6, B4) and lived; the left edge gave it eyes (A7/A9) and a link to C3.
- B6 (cut between B7 and B5-area) had 2 libs and was ataried at once (W B5) -> lost it,
  W connected. Lesson 1 again: a cutting stone with 2 libs next to 3 enemy stones dies.
- Good: G7/G8 then F9 captured F7/F8 and saved the top group (W's 2-lib F-group was the
  weakness). Look for the opponent's weakest group in a race and attack it, rather than
  filling the race libs of a big group that can reach the edge.
- Right edge: W H5 poke + J4/J5/J6 crawl took ~4 points of my side. H4 then J5 was fine, but
  J5 had only 2 libs after W H5 -> lost J5. Block an edge crawl from ABOVE with a 3-lib
  stone (H5 instead of J5, or J5 + H5 together).

4), B F8, W H7 (connect everything), B G9, W B4, B C8, W F1, B A5, W A4, B B5, W J9, pass,
W E1, D1 (captured 10), A1, H1, pass pass.
Takeaways:
- vs tengen + B E3 wedge: both my groups lived on the bottom (left with D3/D4/C2/B2, right
  with G2/G3/H4/J4). Black's wall E2-E5/F4 sat BETWEEN my two living groups = a sandwiched
  wall with eye space only on the 1st line (D1-E1-F1). Lesson 000 works both ways: look for
  the opponent's sandwiched wall and cut its link to open space (here E6/F6/G7 above it).
- Order that worked: D6 (attach on the lone top stone, connected to my wall), E7 (miai
  connection D7/E6), E6, F6 (cut), G7 (seal). Each move was attached to my own strong group,
  so none of them could be cut off.
- Black's eye space D1/E1/F1 had a false eye (D1: diagonal C2 was white) and F1 touched my G1.
  G1 first (solid) made it a clear kill. Capture dead stones before passing (free in area
  scoring) so the engine's dead-stone call can't go wrong.
- Black 14k blundered by ignoring the G7 sealing threat; stronger opponents will defend
  (B G7 or E6 earlier) — still, the plan of living on both sides and pressing the wall is good.

## Game 19 — Black vs 12k — WIN B+24 (captured 12 + 5 stones)
Moves: B C4, W E5, B G6, W C7, B F4, W E4, B E3 (hane under), W F5, B G5 (head of two),
W D4, B D3 (diagonal to C4; covers D3 cut, makes W F3 cut bad), W C5, B C3 (C4 had 2 libs),
W G3 (invasion), B G4 (connects F4 to G5, F4 had 2 libs), W F3, B H3 (block toward my side),
W E2, B D2 (atari), W E1, B G2! (atari F3-G3; W F2 forced), W F2, B D1 (whole group at 1 lib),
W H2, B F1 (captured 5), W G7, B F6 (W center D4-F5 down to 2-3 libs), W E7, B E6 (atari),
W D5, B D6 (2 libs again, cut from E7), W F7?? (ignored), B C6 (atari + cut from C7), W B5,
B B6 (cut from B7), W B7, B B4 (atari), W A6, B A5 (captured 7), W A7, B D7 (split top),
W D8, B H7, W H8, B H6 (cut point), W F8, B J7, W J8, B J2, B H1 (removed H2), pass pass.
Takeaways:
- Same opening as G15 worked again vs W tengen: C4, G6, F4, E3 hane, G5 head.
- Killing a bottom invasion (G3/F3/E2/E1): read the liberties with libs.py and look for the
  atari that forces a connection into a 2-lib shape (G2 -> W F2, then D1 = atari on all 5).
- W's center group was surrounded by my walls on 3 sides: every move I played (F6, E6, D6, C6,
  B6) took a liberty AND cut it from a W top stone. Run libs.py on the OPPONENT's groups
  each move; a 3-lib enemy group touching my strong walls is a target.
